title: What Rhetoric Is
short: Rhetoric is the art of using language to inform, persuade or move an audience. Aristotle defined it as the ability to see, in any case, the available means of persuasion.
trouble: Learners hear rhetoric only as an insult (“empty rhetoric”) and miss that it is the study of how all writing and speech work on an audience.

blocks.html: In Composition you wrote persuasive paragraphs and learned to ask who your reader is and why you are writing. Those two questions are the doorway to rhetoric, one of the oldest subjects in Western schooling.

In the 300s BC the Greek philosopher Aristotle wrote a book called the Rhetoric. He defined rhetoric as “the faculty of observing in any given case the available means of persuasion” (Book I, ch. 2, in W. Rhys Roberts’s translation). In plainer words: for this audience, at this moment, see every honest way you could win them over, and then choose well.

Rhetoric isn’t only for speeches. A lost-cat poster, a cover letter, a museum label and the Gettysburg Address all make rhetorical choices, because each was written for someone, for a reason. Even “plain” writing is a choice: plain words tell a reader that you respect their time.

blocks.name: wr-triangle
blocks.cap: Every text sits inside a situation: a writer, an audience and a message, a purpose in the middle, and a context around them. You will meet each part in the next topic.

blocks.html: Rhetoric is the art of choosing words for an audience and a purpose. Studying it means asking how a text works on its readers, not only what it says.

Every reader is also on the receiving end of persuasion: ads, letters from school, speeches, reviews. Knowing how persuasion works lets you write it well and read it with open eyes. You learn to tell a strong reason from a clever trick, in other people’s writing and in your own.
Aristotle sorted speeches by what the audience is asked to judge. The three kinds still describe most persuasion today.

blocks.title: Rhetoric in an ordinary sign
blocks.q: A sign at a pond: “Please keep dogs on a leash. Our nesting ducks thank you.” What rhetorical choices does it make?
steps: Audience: people walking dogs. Purpose: get them to use a leash.
“Please” is polite. It treats readers as people who will help, not as rule-breakers.
“Our nesting ducks thank you” gives a reason (the ducks are nesting) and a small, friendly picture instead of a threat.
A sign that said “Leash dogs or pay a \$50 fine” could work too, but it would set a colder tone.
blocks.a: The sign persuades with courtesy and a gentle reason. That is rhetoric, even in nine words.

blocks.title: Which kind of speech?
blocks.q: Lincoln spoke at Gettysburg in 1863 to dedicate a cemetery for soldiers killed in the battle there. Which of Aristotle’s kinds is it?
steps: The occasion is a dedication: it honors the dead, so it praises. That is ceremonial.
But the speech also looks ahead: “It is rather for us to be here dedicated to the great task remaining before us.”
Real speeches often blend the kinds. Name the main one, then notice the blend.
blocks.a: Mainly ceremonial (epideictic), with a turn toward future action.

blocks.html: Hearing rhetoric only as an insult. People say “that’s just rhetoric” to mean empty or misleading words. That is one everyday use. The study of rhetoric is much broader: it covers honest, careful persuasion as well as the tricks, and it is how you tell them apart. In this course, read the word as “the art of persuasion,” not “spin.”

blocks.name: wr-sort

cards.text: A town council member argues for a new crosswalk by the school.
A lawyer argues that a contract was broken last May.
A granddaughter’s eulogy praises her grandmother’s kindness.
A student appeals a late penalty by explaining what happened on the due date.
cards.why: It asks the teacher to judge what happened in the past.

cards.text: A graduation speaker honors the class’s hard work.
An editorial urges the library to open on Sundays.
cards.why: It asks readers to decide on a future course of action.

blocks.cap: Sort each speech by what its audience is asked to judge.

blocks.html: Debaters use the same ideas. The Debate chapter Persuasion: Ethos, Pathos and Logos matches Aristotle’s three kinds of speeches to today’s debate formats.
